title: A Sea Goddess Comes Ashore
place: Thian Hock Keng Temple, Telok Ayer Street, Singapore
text: Hokkien migrants who survived the voyage from Fujian used to give thanks at a tiny shrine on the Telok Ayer shoreline, where they first stepped ashore. Between 1839 and 1842 they replaced it with Thian Hock Keng, built with materials shipped from China. In 1840 a statue of Mazu, Goddess of the Seas, arrived in a grand procession. Tan Tock Seng gave 3,000 Spanish dollars, the biggest single gift.

source.name: Roots.sg (National Heritage Board, Singapore): Thian Hock Keng

title: A Tiny Diaspora Builds a Church
place: Armenian Church of St Gregory the Illuminator, Hill Street, Singapore
text: Armenian traders, descended from families moved from Julfa to Persia centuries earlier, reached Singapore by way of India, Java and the Malay ports. Never more than about 100 strong, they still paid $5,058.30 for a church designed by George Coleman, laid down in 1835. It is Singapore's oldest Christian church building. Later community members founded The Straits Times and bred the orchid that became Singapore's national flower.

source.name: BiblioAsia (National Library Board, Singapore): S'pore's Armenian Church Survived Close to 180 Years

title: An 800-Year-Old 'Made in China' Tag
place: Java Sea wreck site, off Indonesia
text: Fishermen found this wreck in the Java Sea in the 1980s. The wooden hull had rotted away, but its cargo remained: an estimated 100,000 ceramics, elephant tusks and blocks of fragrant resin. Two box bases were stamped 'Jianning Fu', a district name the Song government used only from 1162 until 1278. With new radiocarbon dates, that label pushed the sinking back about a century.

source.name: EurekAlert! (Field Museum): Shipwreck and 800-year-old 'made in China' label reveal lost history

title: A Gujarati Anchor on Odisha's Shore
place: Manikapatna, Chilika Lake coast, Puri District, Odisha, India
text: Diggers next to the mosque at Manikapatna, a port on Odisha's Chilika coast, turned up a broken stone anchor of the Indo-Arabian type in 2018 to 2019. Its basalt was no local rock. Chemistry traced it to a lava flow at Palitana in Gujarat, across the subcontinent, perhaps shaped at the port of Ghogha. The same site has yielded Chinese ceramics from the 1200s and 1300s.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Geochemical provenance of an Indo-Arabian stone anchor from Manikapatna

title: Asian Rice on an African Island
place: Sima, Anjouan (Ndzuani), Comoros
text: At Sima, a village site on Anjouan in the Comoros, archaeologists sifted charred seeds from the 700s to 900s. Of 528 crop remains, 481 were Asian rice, plus cotton and mung beans: a Southeast Asian menu, off the coast of Africa. On the nearby mainland, African sorghum and millets ruled. The team argues Austronesian sailors may have settled the Comoros even before Madagascar.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): Ancient crops provide first archaeological signature of the westward Austronesian expansion

title: The Wave Before the 2004 Tsunami
place: Lamreh (Lamri), Aceh Besar, Indonesia
text: Along 40 kilometres of northern Sumatra's coast, tens of thousands of medieval ceramic sherds and over 5,000 carved gravestones tell a grim story. Around 1394 a tsunami wiped out nine trading communities. Only Lamri, perched on a headland, survived. Yet later the low coast was resettled and became the heart of the Aceh Sultanate, the same shore the 2004 tsunami struck.

source.name: PNAS (PMC): A late 14th-century tsunami devastated the coast of northern Sumatra and redirected history

title: A Joseon Tax Ship Comes Up
place: Mado waters, off Taean, South Chungcheong, South Korea
text: Joseon ships hauled grain taxes and official goods up Korea's west coast to the royal capital, Hanyang, today's Seoul. One cargo ship, Mado 4, sank off Taean around 1420. After ten years of study, Korean researchers raised it in 2025 with over 120 artifacts: rice containers, celadon dishes and wooden cargo tags marked with destinations. Its two masts were built for speed.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Joseon Shipwreck Raised from South Korean Waters

title: A Smuggler's Junk Off Nan'ao Island
place: Off Nan'ao Island, Shantou, Guangdong, China
text: In 2007 fishermen off Nan'ao Island secretly hauled up Ming porcelain and hid it, hoping to sell. Border police seized it, and archaeologists found a late Ming junk about 90 feet long, lying 90 feet down. It held over 10,000 blue-and-white pieces, many still stacked, plus bronze cannons. Sailing while the Ming banned private sea trade, its crew were probably smugglers, or worse.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Pirates of the Marine Silk Road

title: Two Ming Ships, a Mile Deep
place: Northwest slope of the South China Sea, Hainan Province, China
text: Nearly 5,000 feet under the South China Sea, about 12 miles apart, lie two Ming ships, one leaving China and one coming back. The older, from the Hongzhi reign (1488 to 1505), held pottery and logs cut from persimmon trees. The younger, from the Zhengde reign (1506 to 1521), carried more than 100,000 porcelain bowls, plates and jars. Together they show the maritime Silk Road flowing both ways.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: 500-Year-Old Shipwrecks Found in South China Sea

title: Persian Wine in a Desert Fort
place: Fulayj fort, near Sohar, Al Batinah, Oman
text: Soldiers at Fulayj, a Sasanian Persian fort about 30 kilometres from the Omani port of Sohar, received tall, pointed 'torpedo jars' lined inside with bitumen. Chemists traced that tar to different provinces of Iran, and residues inside revealed red wine. It is the first published proof of what scholars long suspected: these jars carried wine from Persia's heartlands into the Gulf and Indian Ocean world.

source.name: Molecules (PMC): Origin and Function of Bitumen-Coated Torpedo Jars from the Fort of Fulayj in Oman

title: Indian Cotton in an Arabian Fire
place: Mleiha, Sharjah, United Arab Emirates
text: When a fortified building at Mleiha, an oasis town in today's UAE, burned down around 150 to 250 CE, the fire charred and preserved its stores: barley, dates, lentils, and exotic pepper and Asian rice. Cotton seeds and scraps of cloth lay there too. Strontium in the cotton did not match the Oman peninsula but did match north-western India, likely Gujarat, across the Arabian Sea.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): Strontium isotope evidence for a trade network between southeastern Arabia and India

title: A Sangam Port on the Vaigai
place: Alagankulam, Ramanathapuram District, Tamil Nadu, India
text: Where the Vaigai River nears the sea, Alagankulam thrived as a Tamil port of the Sangam Age, radiocarbon dated from the 300s to the 100s BCE. Diggers found shell-bangle workshops, punch-marked silver coins, luxury black pottery from the distant Ganga plain, Mediterranean wares and Greek and Roman coins. Scientists now read rare earth elements in its soil to map firing and dumping that left no visible trace.

source.name: Heliyon (PMC): Rare earth elements sediment analysis tracing anthropogenic activities at Alagankulam

title: Baghdad's Glass on Zanzibar
place: Unguja Ukuu, Zanzibar, Tanzania
text: Unguja Ukuu, an early Swahili port on Zanzibar, has yielded 3,625 fragments of glass vessels, mostly from the 600s to 800s. Laser analysis of 82 pieces showed some were made with natron, matching Egyptian and Levantine glass, others with plant ash. One group matches glass from Samarra, the Abbasid capital in Iraq. Fragile tableware was crossing thousands of kilometres of ocean as the early Islamic world grew.

source.name: PLOS ONE (PMC): Early Islamic glass (7th-10th centuries AD) in Unguja Ukuu, Zanzibar

title: The Frigate That Failed Fort Jesus
place: Mombasa harbour, below Fort Jesus, Mombasa, Kenya
text: In 1696 an Omani Arab army laid siege to Fort Jesus, Portugal's stronghold at Mombasa. Goa sent a relief squadron of two frigates and two galliots, led by the Santo António de Tanná. In 1697 the frigate was lost off the fort, and Fort Jesus fell to Oman in 1698. Local divers found the wreck; excavations from 1976 to 1980 recovered over 6,000 objects from shipboard life.

source.name: Institute of Nautical Archaeology: Santo Antonio de Tanna Shipwreck Excavation

source2.name: CHAM, NOVA University Lisbon: The Santo António de Tanná project

title: A Royal Navy Frigate Made in Bombay
place: Bombay Dockyard, Mumbai, Maharashtra, India
text: Britain's warships were usually oak, but HMS Trincomalee was built of Malabar teak at the East India Company's dockyard in Bombay, under master shipbuilder Jamsetjee Bomanjee Wadia. Her plans were lost when HMS Java was sunk by the USS Constitution, so a second set took two years to arrive. Launched on 12 October 1817, the frigate still floats today as a museum ship in Hartlepool, England.

source.name: National Historic Ships UK: HMS Trincomalee

source2.name: University of Victoria, Colonial Despatches: HMS Trincomalee

title: Island Graves at the Ocean's Crossroads
place: Soqotra Island, Yemen
text: Medieval islanders on Soqotra buried their dead in tafoni, small rounded caves in the rock. DNA from 39 of them, living between the 600s and 1400s, shows about 86% of their ancestry came from people like those of Yemen's Hadramawt, and about 14% from an Iranian-related source with a trace from India. Surprisingly, despite lying 250 kilometres from the Horn of Africa, they had almost no sub-Saharan African ancestry.

source.name: Nature Ecology & Evolution (PMC): Medieval DNA from Soqotra points to Eurasian origins

title: A Wedding Night Sends the Bugis Sailing
place: Tanjung Pinang, Bintan Island, Riau Islands, Indonesia
text: On 26 December 1819, Bugis guests at a chief's wedding in Riau fired celebratory shots, and the nervous Dutch garrison read it as a threat. Arrests and killings followed. In January 1820 about 400 Bugis besieged the Dutch fort for 15 days before reinforcements broke through. Almost 500 Bugis men, women and children then fled by boat to Singapore, bringing their prized trade with them.

source.name: BiblioAsia (National Library Board, Singapore): The 1820 Uprising in Riau That Brought the Bugis to Singapore

title: Bones of the English Samurai
place: Hirado, Nagasaki Prefecture, Japan
text: William Adams reached Japan in 1600 aboard the Liefde, the last survivor of a five-ship Dutch fleet. Shogun Tokugawa Ieyasu made the English pilot a samurai, Miura Anjin, and he died at the trading port of Hirado in 1620. Foreign graves there were later destroyed. Bones dug up in 2017 carried mitochondrial DNA haplogroup H, common in Europe but never seen in Japanese populations.

source.name: Scientific Reports (PMC): A biomolecular anthropological investigation of William Adams, the first SAMURAI from England

title: Cholera Sails From Calcutta
place: Port of Calcutta, Hooghly River, Kolkata, West Bengal, India
text: Nineteenth-century Calcutta was notorious as a disease port, and British seamen feared its cholera. In February 1854 the ship Sultany left with 80 crew and 375 passengers; by the time it reached Mauritius, 30 were dead. Ship surgeons improvised cures from the spice trade itself, dosing patients with black pepper, ginger and asafoetida mixed with opium, brandy or arrack.

source.name: Medical History (PMC): Cholera, British seamen and maritime anxieties in Calcutta, c.1830s-1890s

title: Fire Ants Ride the Galleons
place: Manila, Luzon, Philippines
text: Tropical fire ants, named for their burning stings, now live around the world. Genetic markers from 192 colonies show they began in the Americas and left in the 1500s. Philippine ants carry a subset of southwestern Mexico's types, and Taiwan's a subset of the Philippines'. The likely ride: ballast soil on Spanish ships from Acapulco to Manila, dumped to make room for silk, porcelain and spices.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ant Explorers

title: Cannonballs Under Old Goa
place: Near the Basilica of Bom Jesus, Old Goa, Goa, India
text: After Afonso de Albuquerque captured Goa in 1510, the Portuguese rebuilt the city as a fortified enclosure. In 2025 builders near the Basilica of Bom Jesus struck a pile of cannonballs marking the old arsenal. It was part of a complex with a gun foundry, mint, stables and naval dockyard that may have employed 700 workers at its sixteenth-century peak. It closed in 1856.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Former Portuguese Colonial Arsenal Unearthed in India

title: Cambodia's 'Dark Age' Was Trading
place: Longvek, Kampong Chhnang, Cambodia
text: After Siam sacked Angkor in 1431, Cambodia's later centuries were often called a dark age. Excavations at the palace of Longvek, a Mekong capital with access to the sea, tell another story. An international team found earthen fortifications, a bronze workshop and porcelain from both China and Japan. As archaeologist Martin Polkinghorne put it, Cambodian history went on, tied closely to international trade.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Excavations at Cambodia's Longvek

title: Bead Workshops Made for Export
place: Vembakottai, Virudhunagar District, Tamil Nadu, India
text: At Vembakottai, a site of the Pandya country in southern Tamil Nadu, three years of digging have produced more than 12,000 artifacts from roughly 300 BCE to 300 CE. Thousands of glass beads and painted shell bangles show it was a major ornament workshop. Locals wore simple terracotta pendants, while the glass and shell pieces were reportedly made only for export, part of Sangam-era trade.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Ancient Shell and Bead Workshop Excavated in Tamil Nadu

title: An Arab-Style Dhow Under a Shrimp Farm
place: Phanom Surin, Samut Sakhon, Thailand
text: Beneath a shrimp farm in Samut Sakhon, near Bangkok, lay the timbers of an 8th- or 9th-century Arab-style dhow, its planks sewn together with rope. It had sunk where a canal or mangrove shore once lay. Inside were ceramics, coconuts, betel nuts, rice, fish and pointed jars never before found in Thailand, of a type carried across the Persian Gulf.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Arab Dhow Unearthed in Thailand

source2.name: Molecules (PMC): Bitumen-Coated Torpedo Jars from Fulayj (cites Phanom-Surin torpedo jars)

title: Card Games on a Mongol Warship
place: Off Takashima Island, Matsuura, Nagasaki, Japan
text: Off Takashima, a third wreck from the Mongol-led Yuan invasion of Japan in 1281 has turned up something unexpected: five dice and 29 small cards for koppai, a Chinese game considered a forerunner of mahjong tiles. The ship, about 100 feet long with living quarters, may have been the fleet's mother ship. The cards were likely used for recreation, a rare glimpse of daily life aboard an invasion fleet.

source.name: Archaeology Magazine: Playing Cards Found in Mongol Invasion Shipwreck off Japan
